units: the sender is staying in an upstairs room of a place that takes travellers in
the message sets out why the party is behind schedule
the planned route follows a line of high ground open to the wind
the unbroken wind costs the walkers more effort
the party slowed its pace
rain the day before had made the stones slippery
the party went round the narrow gorge by another way
the way round lengthens the walk but keeps the danger off
a long rest was taken beside a spring
the exact hour of arrival will be given later
text: I am writing from the upstairs room of the guesthouse, with the route book lying open in front of me. You asked why we are behind, so here is the whole of it. The track we meant to take runs along an open ridge, and the wind up there never drops. It chills the skin and it eats into your strength, so we shortened our stride and walked more slowly than any of us had reckoned on. Then there was the rain of the day before. It had soaked the loose stone all down the slope, and every step slid a little, which is why we went round the narrow gorge rather than push through it. The way round adds a fair stretch to the walk, but it takes the danger out of the day. We also rested a long while beside a spring, longer than any of us had meant to. I shall give you the exact hour of our arrival tomorrow evening.

units: a correspondent asks about the crowding of wild places
the trouble comes of visitors gathering in one spot at one time of year
the most walked path breaks down under repeated tread
one answer is to open further loops reaching the same high ground
those further loops take other flanks of the mountain
booking ahead staggers the arrivals
it keeps the high shelters from being overwhelmed
another line is to make coming outside the busy season a pleasure
that calls for shelters that stay open and transport that can be relied on
explaining how thin the plant cover is cuts down treading off the path
text: A reader asks us what can be done about the crowds wearing out the finest wild places, and the question deserves a proper answer. The trouble is that nearly everyone turns up in the same spot within the same few weeks, so the one favoured path breaks down under the tread. What can be offered instead? Begin by spreading walkers out: waymark further loops that reach the same high ground from other flanks of the mountain. Booking ahead helps as well, since it staggers arrivals and keeps the high shelters from filling past what they can hold. A third answer is to make the quiet months worth choosing, which means huts that stay open and transport that runs when it says it will. The last is simply telling people how thin the plant cover is up there; walkers who know it keep to the path.

units: a walking guide reckons the southern side is the easier one
a woman who works with maps disputes this without heat
the southern path crosses grazing land and rises at an even gradient
that path asks no particular skill of anybody
the northern flank has stony breaks in the slope
the northern flank gives shade all the way and water in quantity
the guide notes that the evening air cools the southern side
she holds that this air comes and goes while trees shelter without a break
the lodging is comfortable on one side and bare on the other
the two of them conclude that the routes come out level
text: The guide kept saying the southern valley walked better than the northern one, and the mapmaker kept disagreeing, quietly. His path, he said, wound through soft grazing land, rose at an even gradient and asked no skill of anybody. She granted him that, then turned him to the far side: broken and stony, yes, but shaded the whole way, with water at every turn. He came back at her with the evening air, which takes the heat out of the southern slope by late afternoon. She answered that such air comes and goes as it pleases, while a wood shelters you without a break. They went on to the beds: a warm inn on one side, a bare hut on the other. He ended by saying it came down to the walker and to what his legs would take. She allowed that the two routes came out level, for opposite reasons.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before dependable surveys, people travelled on the strength of spoken accounts
old accounts of travel turn on three unchanging worries
routes bent towards water even when that lengthened them
a stage with nothing to drink cost travellers dearly
the lie of the land pushed people to work round walls of rock
a high pass was climbed only when it cut the journey short by a good deal
travellers wrote down the places where one slept out of the rain
a lodging thought safe pulled a whole flow of traffic into some valley
the dread of fog and of shifting slopes weighed on the routes as well
such routes look senseless on a survey but answered a need to stay safe
text: Picture the old roads, long before anyone had a dependable survey: you set out on hearsay and little else. The accounts of travel that survive circle round three worries, and they hardly shift from one to the next. Water first. Routes bent towards springs however far it took them, because a stage with nothing to drink was paid for dearly. Then the ground itself. A wall of rock was worked round rather than climbed, unless the pass overhead cut whole days off the way. And lodging: men wrote down carefully where a roof would keep the rain off, and one house with a good name could pull the whole traffic into a valley that had nothing else to recommend it. Add the dread of fog and of shifting scree, and you get lines that look senseless drawn on a map yet answer, all of them, to staying safe.

units: a heap of sand starts up around some very slight obstacle
air carrying grains loses its speed behind that obstacle
the sand it was carrying settles there
the mound rises with every gust
the shape that results has an easy slope on the windward side and an abrupt one opposite
the grains climb the exposed face and drop down the other side
that handover shifts the whole shape little by little
plants taking root pin the sand down
the shape then stops travelling and becomes a fixed rise
text: Where does a dune begin? With almost nothing: a tuft of grass, a pebble, a scrap of driftwood lying on flat sand. Wind loaded with grains slows as soon as it passes behind that small thing, and what it slows it lets go of. A swelling forms, and every fresh gust adds a little more to it. Season upon season the heap grows into a shape of its own, with one long easy slope facing the wind and a short abrupt one in its lee. The grains ride up the exposed face, tip over the crest and slide down the far side. That one steady handover is what carries the whole mass forward, a few paces at a time. Then, once plants take hold, their roots pin the sand down where it lies and the travelling comes to an end. What had been moving becomes a settled hill, one the breeze can no longer redraw at will.

units: the boat started letting water in just after leaving the cove
the current made it impossible to get back to the shore they had left
the two aboard drifted to a shore no survey mentioned
their soaked food had to be left where it lay
that loss sent them up the cliff face towards somewhere inhabited
they came out on a flat top covered with low shrubs
from up there they made out a house standing on its own
the man who worked the farm put them up for two nights
one of them said he owed the finest view of his life to the mishap
text: The boat began to let water in as soon as they had cleared the cove, and that was where the trip turned into something else. There was no rowing back against the current, so the two of them let it carry them to a shingle beach that no survey had bothered with. Their food had swollen with the wet and was fit for nothing, and they left it where it lay. That loss is what sent them up the cliff face to look for people. The climb was long and thirsty, and it opened onto a flat top of heather with the wind running clean across it. From up there they made out a roof of pale tiles, and the wreck turned into a piece of luck. The man who worked the farm put them up for two nights and dried their clothes. One of them said, leaving, that a split hull had bought him the widest view of his life.

units: the piece speaks to anyone whose shoulders ache from the first climb onwards
the first move is to tip the whole contents out on flat ground
the belongings are sorted into three heaps according to how far they are needed
the useless heap goes, with no argument
what is kept should weigh no more than a fifth of what the walker weighs
heavy things go against the back and high up
a load carried too low pulls the walker backwards
the hip belt is pulled tight before the shoulder straps
the setting is checked on a short descent
a strap that hurts should be let out a notch before another try
text: Do your shoulders start complaining on the first climb of the day? Then work through this. Tip the pack out on flat ground, the whole of it, and sort what comes out into three heaps: what you cannot do without, what earns its place, and what does not. Get rid of the third heap and do not argue with yourself about it. Weigh what is left; it should come to no more than a fifth of what you weigh. Pack the heavy things against your back and high up, level with the shoulder blades, since weight riding low pulls you backwards and unsteadies you on loose stone. Pull the hip belt tight before you touch the shoulder straps, because the hips must carry the bulk of it. Then go and test the setting on a short descent that you can run down. If a strap bites, let it out a notch and try again.

units: two valleys side by side settled on opposite ways of taking visitors in
one put its money into road works and structures for crossing water
the number of visitors there has doubled
trade has set itself up there
the people living there complain of a noise that never stops in the busy season
the other valley closed the drivable track above the last inhabited place
visitors get in on foot or by shared transport
earnings there rise more gently
the wearing away of the riverbanks has eased and the quiet draws people
neither valley is thinking of turning back
text: Two valleys side by side took opposite roads on the question of visitors, and the difference now shows on the ground. The first spent its money on getting people in: a widened road, a car park cut into terraces, metal footbridges thrown across the torrents. Numbers there have doubled, shops have opened, and those who live in the valley speak of a hum that never stops through the busy months. The second closed the drivable track above the last hamlet, so that anyone going higher walks or rides the shuttle. Earnings climb more gently there, but the riverbanks have stopped wearing away and the quiet has become the thing that draws people. The councillors of both valleys call on one another often. Each of them sees in the other what he most dreads. Neither talks yet of turning back.

units: the high ground described comes in successive levels of differing character
grazing land holds the foot of it, quartered by hedges
a path of pale sand threads between the enclosures
higher up the ground dries out and the plants keep low
grey rock breaks through there in patches
a wall of stone laid without mortar runs along the crest for a great distance
that wall once served to steer the herds
the top is open to the wind and carries a smell of stone
two shallow stretches of water there bring down birds on passage
the far side drops into a wooded hollow with a resting place
text: The plateau gives itself away in steps, and each step has a look of its own. At the foot lies grazing land, quartered by low hedges, with a path of pale sand threading between the enclosures and the drinking troughs. Higher up the heath takes over: the ground dries out, the plants keep close to it, and grey rock breaks through in patches. A wall of stone laid without mortar runs along the crest for a great distance; it was raised long ago to steer the herds to the summer grazing. At the top the wind has nothing to push against, and the air carries a smell of stone. Two shallow pools hold the rainwater and bring down birds on passage. On the far side, last of all, a wooded slope drops into a closed hollow, where a resting place offers a bench, a timber shelter and a spring caught under a slab.

units: the writer holds that the way we travel has slipped by degrees
at the start you went out walking along a river with no fixed plan
you came home tired with very few pictures
then came the lists of places one absolutely had to see
the device worked its way in between the traveller and the country
a mountain pass is now looked at through a lens
walkers come down a glorious path with their eyes on nothing
they hurry towards a viewpoint picked out beforehand
the writer does not want some golden age brought back
he asks only for a halt with no purpose, for the pleasure of breathing
text: We have let travelling go to seed, and it happened by degrees. At first you went out to walk. You followed a river, slept wherever the day ran out, came home with hard calves and two blurred pictures. Then came the lists: the places you absolutely had to see, ranked, scored, ticked off one by one. After that a screen slid in between us and the country, and we took to looking at a pass through a lens before looking at it at all. Now you meet people coming down a glorious path with their eyes on nothing, in a hurry to reach the viewpoint they picked out the night before. I am not asking for some golden age to be brought back; those old rambles were badly prepared as often as not. I ask only that we let ourselves halt for no purpose, in the middle of nowhere, for the pleasure of breathing.
